entities.title: Ireland - Immigration and work authorisation (third-country professional)

facts.fact_text: A non-EEA professional whose occupation sits on the Critical Skills Occupations List does NOT need the employer to run a Labour Market Needs Test. This is the structural advantage of the Critical Skills Employment Permit (CSEP) over the General Employment Permit, which does require the test and the 4-week advertising cycle it brings.
facts.evidence_quote: Because the skills are identified as being in short supply, a Labour Market Needs Test is not required.

facts.fact_text: CSEP eligibility for a non-EEA professional turns on occupation plus annual remuneration: EUR 40,904 for Critical Skills Occupations List roles with a relevant degree; EUR 36,848 where the qualification was obtained in the 12 months before application; EUR 68,911 for occupations not on the list. Only basic salary and registered health insurance payments count toward the threshold.
facts.evidence_quote: Occupations with a minimum annual remuneration of €40,904 for a restricted number of strategically important occupations contained in the Critical Skills Occupations List a relevant degree qualification or higher is required.

facts.fact_text:
Every employment permit application must reach DETE at least 12 weeks before the proposed employment start date. For a non-EEA professional this 12 weeks is only the FIRST leg of the runway: where an entry visa is also needed, the visa application can only follow the permit grant.

Commonly believed: You apply for the permit once you have accepted the job offer.

Actually: The 12-week minimum is a DETE intake rule, not a processing estimate, and it runs before any visa or registration step. A start date agreed with the employer inside 12 weeks of the offer cannot lawfully be met through this route.

Action required: Fix the permit lodgement date first and work the agreed start date backwards from it.
facts.evidence_quote: An application for any employment permit must be received at least 12 weeks before the proposed employment start date.

facts.fact_text:
The employment permit authorises the WORK, not the residence. A non-EEA professional holding a valid CSEP is still not lawfully resident until the permission is registered and an Irish Residence Permit is issued.

Commonly believed: The employment permit is the document that lets you live and work in Ireland.

Actually: Permit (DETE) and residence permission (Department of Justice) are two separate authorisations from two separate authorities. Holding only the permit and skipping registration leaves the person unlawfully present while working.

Action required: Treat registration as a mandatory second authorisation, not paperwork - book it immediately on arrival.
facts.evidence_quote: An employment permit is not a Residence Permission. In order to be lawfully resident in the State, it is a requirement that all non-EEA nationals in possession of an employment permit must register with the Garda National Immigration Bureau.

facts.fact_text:
A permit for a non-EEA professional is refused unless 50% or more of the employer's workforce are EEA nationals when the application is made. The applicant's own eligibility is therefore not sufficient - the employer's headcount composition is a gating condition the candidate cannot influence.

Commonly believed: Permit eligibility is about the applicant's qualifications and salary.

Actually: The 50:50 rule is an EMPLOYER-side test. A small or newly-founded Irish entity staffed mainly by non-EEA nationals cannot sponsor, regardless of how well the candidate qualifies. Start-ups within 2 years of establishment that are Enterprise Ireland or IDA Ireland clients may have it waived.

Action required: Confirm with the employer that they meet the 50:50 test, or hold the waiver, before resigning the current role.
facts.evidence_quote: An employment permit will not be granted to companies unless 50% or more of the employees in the firm are EEA nationals at the time of application.

facts.fact_text: The CSEP processing fee is EUR 1,000, of which 90% is refunded if the application is unsuccessful. Where the employer is the applicant, the employer may not deduct or recover any application charge, fee or expense from the permit holder's remuneration.
facts.evidence_quote: The processing fee for a Critical Skills Employment Permit is €1,000. If an application is unsuccessful then 90% of the fee will be refunded.

facts.fact_text: CONDITIONAL FACT - the visa-required determination is not asserted here. DETE states the sequence: if the national is visa-required, the entry visa application follows the successful employment permit application and is made to the local Irish Embassy or Consulate. Whether a given nationality is visa-required is governed by the ISD visa-required nationality list (batch ie-isd-visa-required-2026-08-22); this record asserts only the ORDERING, not the status of any nationality.

applies_to.conditional_on: ie-isd-visa-required-2026-08-22 (task A3) determines whether a given nationality is visa-required; this record asserts sequence only.

facts.evidence_quote: Following a successful application for an employment permit, and if visa required, an applicant should apply to his/her local Irish Embassy/Consulate for an entry Visa.

facts.fact_text:
A new employment permit for a DIFFERENT employer cannot be considered until 9 months have elapsed since the holder first commenced employment in the State under an employment permit. Redundancy, and unforeseen circumstances that fundamentally change the employment relationship, are the stated exceptions.

Commonly believed: The 2-year job offer is the commitment; you can move employer if a better role appears.

Actually: Statute (section 18, Employment Permits Regulations 2024) blocks a different-employer permit for the first 9 months. For a mover who has already relocated a household, the first 9 months carry no employer mobility at all.

Action required: Treat the first 9 months as employer-locked when weighing the offer and the move.
facts.evidence_quote: In accordance with section 18 of the Employment Permits Regulations 2024, a new employment permit (for a different employer) cannot be considered if less than 9 months has elapsed since the permit holder first commenced employment in the State pursuant to an employment permit.

facts.fact_text: At the end of the CSEP's duration the holder does not renew the permit through DETE. They apply directly to the Department of Justice for a Stamp 4, which permits residence and work without any employment permit. Since 30 November 2023 no DETE Stamp 4 Support Letter is required. Holders who do not satisfy the criteria receive a Stamp 1 and continue to need a permit.
facts.evidence_quote: Instead, Critical Skills Employment Permit can apply directly to the Dept of Justice for a Stamp 4. Please note as of 30 November 2023 a Stamp 4 Support Letter from the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment is no longer required.

facts.fact_text: A national of a country outside the EU, UK or Switzerland who comes to Ireland to work for more than 90 days must register their immigration permission with Immigration Service Delivery. Registration is what records the permission and what the holder may lawfully do.
facts.evidence_quote: If you are from a country outside the European Union, UK or Switzerland, and come to Ireland to work, study, live or join family for more than 90 days, you must register with Immigration Service Delivery.

facts.fact_text: On admission at the port of entry the passport is endorsed with a landing stamp, and that stamp instructs registration with ISD within 90 days. The deadline is set by the stamp at arrival, not by the permit or the visa.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: When you first arrive in Ireland and are permitted to enter, your passport will be endorsed with a landing stamp. The landing stamp will instruct that you register with Immigration Service Delivery within 90 days.

facts.fact_text:
Appointments can only be booked after arrival in the State, once the instruction to register has been received. The 90-day clock and the appointment queue therefore both start on landing and cannot be pre-empted from Madrid.

Commonly believed: You can arrange your immigration appointment in advance, like a visa appointment.

Actually: ISD will not accept a booking made before arrival. Nothing about the registration step can be front-loaded, so the queue is entered cold on day one of a 90-day deadline.

Action required: Plan to create the ISD portal account and book on the day of arrival.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: Appointments should only be booked after you receive an instruction to register, on arrival in the State.

facts.fact_text: Burgh Quay Registration Office in Dublin city centre is the single nationwide office where every first-time registration appointment takes place, at 13/14 Burgh Quay, Dublin 2, D02 XK70. A Dublin-based arrival is at the office; an arrival anywhere else in the State must still travel to Dublin for it.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: Burgh Quay Registration Office, located in Dublin City Centre is the nationwide Registration Office for Ireland where all first time registration appointments take place.

facts.fact_text: The first-time registration fee is EUR 300 per person, payable by credit or debit card only (contactless accepted). Employment-permit stamps - Stamp 1 and Stamp 4 - both carry the EUR 300 fee. Booking the appointment itself is free.
facts.evidence_quote: The registration fee is €300 (per person), if applicable. You can pay this fee by credit or debit card only.

facts.fact_text:
Where no appointment slot is available inside the 90 days, a successfully BOOKED appointment made within the 90 days of arrival is sufficient to remain in the State until the appointment date.

Commonly believed: If you cannot get an appointment within 90 days you fall out of permission.

Actually: The booking, not the appointment, is what has to happen inside 90 days. This is the single most reassuring registration fact and it is not on the main registration page.

Action required: Book as early as possible and retain the booking confirmation as evidence of lawful presence until the appointment.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: Once you have successfully booked an appointment within the 90 days of arrival, this will be sufficient to remain in the state until the date of your appointment.

facts.fact_text:
CONDITIONAL FACT - ISD states that a visa-required national who leaves the State before their registration appointment cannot re-enter without a new entry visa. Whether a given nationality is visa-required is governed by the ISD visa-required nationality list (batch ie-isd-visa-required-2026-08-22); this record asserts only the CONSEQUENCE for a national who is visa-required.

Commonly believed: You can travel in and out of Ireland freely once you have arrived on your visa and permit.

Actually: The entry visa is typically single-entry until the permission is registered. A weekend back in Madrid before the Burgh Quay appointment can strand a visa-required national outside the State.

Action required: Do not leave Ireland between arrival and the registration appointment.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration
applies_to.conditional_on: ie-isd-visa-required-2026-08-22 (task A3) determines whether a given nationality is visa-required; this record asserts the consequence only.

facts.evidence_quote: Note: If you are a visa-required national and you leave the state prior to your registration appointment, you will not be able to re-enter the state without a new entry visa.

facts.fact_text:
A residence permit cannot be held for more than one EU country at a time. For a third-country professional moving from Spain, the existing Spanish residence authorisation and an Irish residence permission are mutually exclusive.

Commonly believed: You keep your Spanish residence card as a fallback while you settle in Ireland.

Actually: ISD states a residence permit cannot be held for more than one EU country at a time. Registering in Ireland is a decision about the Spanish permission too - and the years of Spanish residence do not transfer, because Ireland is outside Schengen and is not bound by the EU Long-Term Residents Directive.

Action required: Take advice on the Spanish permission BEFORE registering in Ireland; this is a two-jurisdiction decision, not an Irish formality.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: In addition, you cannot hold a residence permit for more than one EU country at a time.

facts.fact_text: At the appointment the documents are reviewed, a photograph and fingerprints are taken, the passport is stamped with the permission granted, and the EUR 300 fee may be payable. The visit takes no longer than 60 minutes. The photograph and personal details are used on the Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card, which evidences the conditions of lawful residence.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: Your documents will be reviewed your photograph and fingerprints taken. Your passport will be stamped with the permission to reside granted. You may be required to pay the registration fee of €300 to register your immigration permission. The visit should take no longer than 60 minutes.

facts.fact_text: Permission registered on the basis of an employment permit is usually valid for 12 months and is renewable subject to qualifying conditions. Renewals and stamp changes are completed by online application, not at Burgh Quay. Permission should be renewed at least one month before expiry to avoid unlawful presence.
facts.evidence_quote: Registration granted to persons to work based on an Employment Permit is usually valid for 12 months, thereafter the permission may be renewed subject to qualifying conditions.

facts.fact_text:
Counting holidays plus personal and work-related travel, absence from the State should not exceed 90 days in a rolling year for an IRP holder.

Commonly believed: Once you hold an IRP you can travel as much as your job requires.

Actually: ISD applies a 90-day-in-a-rolling-year absence expectation, and heavy business travel or extended returns to family abroad can erode the residence record that later long-term residence and naturalisation applications rest on.

Action required: Keep a running total of days outside the State from the first day of permission.

applies_to.source_name: ISD - Frequently asked questions for Registration

facts.evidence_quote: Between holidays, personal and work related travel, absence from the state should not exceed 90 days in a rolling year.

facts.fact_text: A PPS Number is only issued where it is needed to access a public service. Starting a job qualifies, because tax cannot be paid without it. Looking for work does not qualify. A third-country professional therefore cannot obtain the number on the strength of arriving - the signed employment is the trigger.

applies_to.source_name: DSP / MyWelfare - Personal Public Service (PPS) Number

facts.evidence_quote: You can only get a PPS Number if you need one to access public services. For example, if you are starting a job you will need a PPS Number to pay tax. You do not need a PPS Number if you are looking for work.

facts.fact_text: The PPS Number application starts online through MyWelfare, but all residents of Ireland must attend an in-person appointment to complete it. The appointment is booked as part of the online application, and the required-document list is issued with the booking confirmation.

applies_to.source_name: DSP / MyWelfare - Personal Public Service (PPS) Number

facts.evidence_quote: All residents of Ireland are required to attend an in-person PPS Number appointment as part of your application.

facts.fact_text:
The application is not processed at the in-person appointment. It undergoes further checks afterwards and, if successful, the number is posted at a later date.

Commonly believed: You walk out of the PPS appointment with your number.

Actually: Nothing is issued on the day and no processing time is published. The gap between the appointment and the letter is exactly the window in which Emergency Tax accrues, because the employer cannot obtain an RPN without the number.

Action required: Book the PPS appointment in the first days after arrival and warn the employer's payroll that the first pay runs may be on the emergency basis.

applies_to.source_name: DSP / MyWelfare - Personal Public Service (PPS) Number

facts.evidence_quote: During the in-person appointment, your application will not be processed immediately. It will undergo further checks after the appointment. If your application is successful, your PPS Number will be sent to you via post at a later date.

facts.fact_text: The MyWelfare PPS Number service cannot be reached without first registering a basic MyGovID account. This is a separate identity registration that has to be completed before the PPS application can even be started.

applies_to.source_name: DSP / MyWelfare - Personal Public Service (PPS) Number

facts.evidence_quote: You must register for a basic MyGovID account to access this service.

facts.fact_text: Revenue does not issue PPS Numbers. Where the arriving professional has no PPSN, Revenue directs them to the Department of Social Protection; only once the number exists can they register for myAccount and add the first job. Two agencies, in a fixed order: DSP then Revenue.
facts.evidence_quote: If you do not have a PPSN, then you must contact the Department of Social Protection (DSP).

facts.fact_text: Emergency Tax is an alternative basis of deduction applied when the employer cannot obtain a Revenue Payroll Notification for the employee. Avoiding it requires two things together: the employer holding the PPSN, and the job being registered with Revenue.
facts.evidence_quote: Income Tax and Universal Social Charge (USC) are deducted from your gross pay at the Emergency Tax rates by your employer. This happens in certain circumstances where your employer is unable to get a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) for you.

facts.fact_text: Where the employee has not provided a PPSN to the employer, all pay is taxed at the higher rate of 40% from the first payroll run - with no rate band and no credits.
facts.evidence_quote: Your employer will tax all your pay at the higher rate of tax (40%).

facts.fact_text: Where the PPSN HAS been given but the job is not registered, a single person's rate band is allowed for the first four weeks of employment: 20% up to the weekly rate band, 40% above it.
facts.evidence_quote: Where you have provided your PPSN, you are allowed a single person’s rate band for the first four weeks of employment.

facts.fact_text:
The four-week concession expires. From week 5 onwards the employee's FULL income is taxed at the higher rate of 40%, even though the PPSN was provided, for as long as the job remains unregistered and no RPN exists.

Commonly believed: Emergency tax is a small first-payslip annoyance that sorts itself out.

Actually: It escalates on a statutory clock. Weeks 1-4 keep a single person's rate band; from week 5 the whole of gross pay is taxed at 40% plus emergency USC. For a professional salary that is a very large cash-flow hit landing in the same weeks as Dublin rental deposits.

Action required: Register the job in Revenue myAccount within the first four weeks - the week-5 cliff, not the first payslip, is the real deadline.
facts.evidence_quote: From Week 5 onwards, your full income will be taxed at the higher rate (40%).

facts.fact_text:
For any later job the employer registers the employment. For a first job in the State the employee must register it themselves in Revenue myAccount under PAYE Services.

Commonly believed: Payroll onboarding handles your tax registration, as it does for colleagues.

Actually: Revenue splits the duty by whether it is the person's first employment in Ireland. On a first Irish job the employer CANNOT register it - only the employee can, through myAccount. Both sides assuming the other will do it is the ordinary way movers reach the week-5 40% cliff.

Action required: Register for Revenue myAccount and add the job yourself under PAYE Services; do not wait for payroll.
facts.evidence_quote: Your employer needs to register your employment if it is not your first job. If it is your first job in the State, you can register your job on myAccount, by clicking ‘Add Job or Pension Details’ under ‘PAYE Services’.

facts.fact_text: Once the first job is registered, Revenue makes a Revenue Payroll Notification available to the new employer, which the employer uses to calculate Income Tax and USC. The RPN is the output of the employee's registration - the employer cannot conjure it.
facts.evidence_quote: When you have registered your first job, Revenue will make a Revenue Payroll Notification (RPN) available to your new employer. Your employer will use the RPN to calculate how much Income Tax and Universal Social Charge (USC) to deduct from your pay.

facts.fact_text: On the emergency basis, USC is charged at a flat rate - 8% in 2026 - on all income, on top of the Income Tax deducted at the emergency rates. The headline 40% understates the total deduction.
facts.evidence_quote: The emergency rate of USC is a flat percentage rate (8% in 2026) applied to all income.

facts.fact_text: Entitlement to a Medical Card or GP Visit Card rests on being ordinarily resident in the State, which HSE defines as living here and intending to live here for at least one year. It is open to anyone ordinarily resident, in or out of work - so for a third-country professional the test is residence and intention, not nationality and not contribution history.

applies_to.source_name: HSE - National Assessment Guidelines for Medical Card and GP Visit Card

facts.evidence_quote: Anyone who is ‘ordinarily resident’ in the Republic of Ireland can apply for a Medical Card or GP Visit Card. This includes families, single people, including those working full or part-time or not at all. ‘Ordinarily resident’ means that you are living here and intend to live here for at least one year.

facts.fact_text:
Where the applicant is a non-EU/EEA or Swiss national, the HSE may contact the immigration service for copies of documents proving ordinary residence, or that the applicant's permission allows them to apply at all. This is an extra, nationality-triggered evidential step that an EEA applicant does not face.

Commonly believed: A medical card application is a means test.

Actually: For a non-EEA applicant the HSE adds an immigration-status check and may go directly to the immigration authorities. The residence permission itself becomes part of the health application, so an unregistered or lapsed permission can block health entitlement.

Action required: Do not apply for the card until the IRP is issued, and keep the permission documents with the health paperwork.

applies_to.source_name: HSE - National Assessment Guidelines for Medical Card and GP Visit Card
applies_to.quote_normalization: Source is a PDF-derived HSE guideline; bullet glyphs and soft line-wraps were removed. No word was added, dropped or reordered.

facts.evidence_quote: We may contact the Irish Naturalisation and Immigration Service (INIS) to get copies of documents that prove: you and your dependants are ordinarily resident or your visa permits you to apply for a Medical Card or GP Visit Card.

facts.fact_text: The application requires evidence that the applicant owns or rents accommodation and that it is their family home. A newly-arrived professional in temporary or short-let Dublin accommodation may be unable to evidence ordinary residence until a permanent tenancy is in place - which chains health entitlement to the housing step.

applies_to.source_name: HSE - National Assessment Guidelines for Medical Card and GP Visit Card

facts.evidence_quote: As part of your application, you will have to provide evidence that you own or rent accommodation and it is your family home.

facts.fact_text: Irish tax status is not a single question. A person can be resident, ordinarily resident, domiciled, or any combination of the three, and the combination decides what income is chargeable. A third-country professional arriving mid-year will typically hold a different combination in the arrival year than in later years.
facts.evidence_quote: You can be resident, ordinarily resident, domiciled or any combination of the three.

facts.fact_text:
Once resident AND domiciled in Ireland for tax purposes, the person is chargeable to Irish tax on worldwide income - the total earned anywhere in the world in the tax year - subject to relief under an applicable Double Taxation Agreement.

Commonly believed: You pay Irish tax on your Irish salary.

Actually: The charge follows residence and domicile, not the source of the money. Spanish rental income, investments or trailing Spanish employment income can fall into the Irish charge, with the Ireland-Spain Double Taxation Agreement as relief rather than exemption.

Action required: List every non-Irish income source before the first Irish return and take advice on the DTA position.
facts.evidence_quote: If you are resident and domiciled in Ireland for tax purposes, you are chargeable to tax in Ireland on your worldwide income. Worldwide income is the total income that you earn anywhere in the world in a tax year. This is subject to any relief due under the terms of a relevant Double Taxation Agreement.

facts.fact_text:
A person can be non-resident for Irish tax purposes while still being ordinarily resident and domiciled, and that combination changes what income remains chargeable to Irish tax. The Irish tax relationship therefore outlasts the physical move in both directions.

Commonly believed: Tax follows where you live: leave Ireland and the Irish charge stops.

Actually: Ordinary residence and domicile persist after residence ends, so Irish tax exposure can continue for years after departure - which matters for a professional treating Dublin as one posting in a longer international career.

Action required: Model the exit position at the same time as the arrival position, not when leaving.
facts.evidence_quote: You might be non-resident in Ireland for tax purposes, but ordinarily resident and domiciled. This will affect what income is chargeable to Irish tax.
